subject: Peregrine private pool: capacity binding & egress split planning

Cc: Maya Singh <procurement@peregrine.com>

Subject: New capacity ask — Peregrine private pool throughput profile and egress constraints

Hi David,

Thanks again for taking this on. We finished a first pass at the traffic profile and attached the CSV (Peregrine_Traffic_Profile.csv). High level:
- Steady-state inference demand: ~6k tokens/sec (all models combined)
- Typical batch shape: 85% small requests (~60 tokens), 15% large (~1.2k tokens)
- Peak windows (10–15 min): up to 32k tokens/sec during marketing events
- 95th pct latency target: <= 200ms for the default chat route

Primary asks:
1) What GPU pool sizing would Redwood recommend for sustained 6k tps with the headroom to absorb 32k bursts while staying inside lat SLO?
2) We're constrained on cross-connects — max egress per xconnect is 8 Gbps. Suggest an egress split approach so we don't get blocked.
3) Timeline: procurement wants numbers this week so they can lock procurement windows and lead times.

Attachments: Peregrine_Traffic_Profile.csv

Thanks,
Sanjay Rao
Head of Platform Reliability, Peregrine Systems
ops+peregrine@example.com

Subject: Re: New capacity ask — Peregrine private pool throughput profile and egress constraints

Sanjay — thanks for the profile. I pulled the numbers into a quick model (attached). High level proposal below; I kept the plan conservative so your ops team has headroom during the first 90d.

Summary recommendation (initial deployment):
- Pool hardware: 8 x A100 80GB-equivalent GPUs (or 10 x 40GB-class equivalent depending on your rack limits).
- Expected sustained throughput: ~7k tokens/sec at 95th latency <150ms (with batching + prefix caching).
- Burst absorption: pool can absorb short peaks up to ~28–32k tokens/sec for ~10 minutes before admission gating starts to shed noncritical routes.
- Warm pool: reserve capacity of 1–2 GPUs for warmup to reduce cold-start latency for large requests.

Networking / egress split:
- Split egress across two cross-connects; balance RPS by weighted routing (70/30 primary/secondary).
- Implement egress throttles per route and an emergency gate that sends non-prod traffic to a degraded, lower-cost model variant.

Operational controls we recommend we include in SOW:
- Canary rollout (5% -> 25% -> 100%) with perf monitoring and automatic rollback on 2x baseline latency breach.
- Admission control curve (see tab "AdmissionCurve" in attached workbook).

I've attached dk_peregrine_capacity_model_v1.xlsx and a draft egress topology (egress_topology_draft.pdf). If that looks good I can hand this to Marissa to start procurement numbers and SOW drafting.

—David

On Tue, Sep 5, 2028 at 11:00 AM, David Kim <david_kim@redwood.com> wrote:
> I've attached dk_peregrine_capacity_model_v1.xlsx and a draft egress topology (egress_topology_draft.pdf).

Thanks David — a few items from an ops/readiness perspective:
- Warm pool sizing: start with 1 GPU dedicated to warm prefix/KV cache; plan to add a second if cache hit rates are <60% after 30d. Cache warmup gives us ~12–18% token reduction for Peregrine's mix in our sims.
- Canary & rollback: add a canary health check on token-level SLOs plus an end-to-end synthetic user journey that exercises the large-request path.
- Egress resiliency: given 8 Gbps per xconnect, plan the primary xconnect for normal traffic and configure the secondary to accept overflow + large-file responses (we should classify responses >100kB as overflow candidates).

Operational ask for Peregrine: please confirm whether encrypted backups will be staged to your S3 (you listed internal retention 30d) — affects egress budgeting.

I'll follow up with a short ops playbook excerpt to include in the SOW if you want.

—Laura
Laura Bennett

A few deeper numbers from the runtime side that feed into David's model (refer to "AdmissionCurve" and "RuntimeAssumptions" tabs):
- Prefix/KV caching: with your workload distribution we see ~18% average token traffic reduction after warmup (large requests benefit the most).
- Batching strategy: target dynamic batching with a 40ms max batch delay for default route — yields ~1.7x throughput improvement on A100-class GPUs for small/med mixes.
- Admission control shaping: recommend smoothing bursts >20k tps over a 60s window with a leaky-bucket that enforces 30k tps hard cap to protect tail latency.
- Fallback model: a 4-bit quantized L2 variant gives ~3.8x throughput for heavy queries but increases nondeterministic output variance — plan it as a last-resort degraded-quality path (annotate responses).

Operational implication: with these tactics the 8x A100 pool can meet steady-state and short bursts but you should plan a staged 2–4 week scale exercise post-cutover to validate real-world burst behavior.

—Jonas
Jonas Weber
Principal Systems Engineer, Runtime
Redwood Inference
